analysis.one_liner: Lets student loan borrowers discharge their loans in bankruptcy under a plain "hardship" standard instead of "undue hardship."
analysis.headline: The bill, which would make student debt dischargeable in bankruptcy under a "hardship" standard, has sat in the House Judiciary Committee since its July 2025 referral with no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, student loans are one of the hardest debts to wipe out in bankruptcy: a borrower must prove an "undue hardship," a standard most courts apply through the Brunner test, which succeeds in fewer than 0.1% of attempts. This bill would delete one word — striking "undue" from the bankruptcy code — leaving a "hardship" standard and letting judges decide case by case, while keeping the normal bankruptcy requirements like means testing. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and has seen no action since.
analysis.who_benefits: Distressed student loan borrowers — the bill's findings describe around 43 million federal student loan holders, 20% of them in default — who file for bankruptcy and want a realistic chance to discharge unpayable loans and get a fresh start. Courts would also gain flexibility to develop more workable criteria than the decades-old Brunner test.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Struggling student loan borrowers in bankruptcy

how_it_helps.text: Striking "undue" from the bankruptcy code's student-loan exception leaves a "hardship" standard, which the bill's findings say would give courts flexibility to replace the Brunner test — a standard under which only about 0.01% of discharge attempts succeeded as of 2022 [S2].

The findings state that a majority of borrowers with loans 90 days past due could move into default, and that credit-score damage is making loans, insurance, and credit cards more expensive for them [S2].
The bill keeps all other bankruptcy safeguards — means testing, disclosure requirements, and exemption limits — so discharge still requires a genuine insolvency, per the findings [S2].
The change applies to bankruptcy cases filed before, on, or after enactment, so borrowers already in bankruptcy could benefit immediately [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Education lenders and loan-holding entities that currently enjoy the near-unguaranteed protection of a discharge-proof loan would face real risk of losing money in bankruptcy. The federal government could book larger losses on discharged federal loans, though the findings argue much of this debt was never going to be repaid anyway. Lenders may respond by tightening credit or raising rates on student loans.

drawbacks.text: Because the standard applies to federal loans, discharges transfer losses to the Treasury — a cost the findings partly offset by arguing that much of this debt is "often never paid" anyway [S2].

Loans that are easier to discharge are riskier to make, so private lenders and schools' financing arms could respond with tighter underwriting, higher rates, or smaller loan volumes — potentially raising costs for future borrowers.

The "hardship" standard is deliberately open-ended, leaving outcomes dependent on which circuit and judge a borrower draws, at least until appellate courts settle the criteria; the bill's findings acknowledge courts would need to develop new criteria [S2].

Retroactive application to cases already commenced — unusual in bankruptcy legislation — gives currently pending cases new rights mid-stream, which creditors would argue disrupts settled expectations [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers in genuine distress the benefit is real: bankruptcy exists to give honest debtors a fresh start, and the current standard, by the record's own numbers, is a near-absolute bar rather than a screen for abuse. The main costs fall on lenders and potentially taxpayers through discharged federal loans, and the vagueness of "hardship" will produce uneven results until courts settle it. The bill does nothing to address the cost of college itself, so it relieves past debts without fixing future ones.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in July 2025 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote ever since.

narrative.text: Representative Luis Correa and 15 original cosponsors introduced the bill on July 16, 2025, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S1] [S2] [S4].
The cosponsor list has since grown to 24 members, all Democrats, with no Republican support on record [S3].
The full action history shows no action beyond the initial referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing has happened yet, so nobody has gained or lost anything. If the bill continues to sit, the status quo favors student lenders and the debt collection industry, which keep loans that a bankruptcy judge could otherwise erase.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the status quo persists

for.name: Rep. J. Luis Correa
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strike "undue" from the student loan bankruptcy discharge standard.

for.name: 24 Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support; none of the 24 is a Republican.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in July 2025 and has taken no action — no hearing or markup — through the present.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 24 cosponsors are Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors on record; the bill sits in a committee chaired by the majority party without action.

industries.industry: Student loan servicers and debt collectors
industries.note: Their business depends on loans that cannot be erased in bankruptcy; the findings note servicers and collectors depend on a standard under which almost no discharge ever succeeds, and easier discharge directly shrinks collectible debt [S2]. A borrower's relief is these firms' lost revenue, so their interest runs against the public's in this bill.

Dischargeable loans carry real risk of loss, which lenders would price in through rates and underwriting. The bill's findings counter that much of this debt is uncollectible anyway, so some of the "loss" is on paper only [S2].

analysis.trajectory: The bill has one party's support and has sat untouched in the House Judiciary Committee since July 2025. Private-member bankruptcy bills without bipartisan cosponsors or a committee hearing almost never reach the floor; the realistic path is that it stays pending until the Congress ends unless the committee schedules action.
